text: A payment of €1,500 per annum for 15 years will be made to affected turf-cutters who have ceased cutting on raised bog SACs.
The Cessation of Turf Cutting Compensation Scheme provides annual payments of €1,500 to eligible turf-cutters.
Funding of €10 million per annum will be allocated to peatland restoration under the Nature for Climate Fund.
Compensation packages of up to €500 per hectare will be available to landowners who enter into peatland restoration agreements.
The government will provide €20 million in 2021-22 through the Farming in Protected Landscapes Programme.
An annual payment of €2,000 will be provided to farmers who maintain peatland habitats in good condition.
The State paid over €25 million to purchase land rights for over 2,400 hectares of raised bog.
Grants of up to €5,000 per hectare will be available for peatland restoration projects under the new scheme.
The compensation scheme will provide a once-off incentive payment of €500 upon signing of the legal agreement.
Financial support of €8 million has been invested in peatland restoration in 2020/21.
An aggregate reduction in CO2 emissions of at least 80% compared to 1990 levels by 2050 is required.
Peatland restoration will enable our peatlands to meet their Net Zero contribution by 2050.
Ireland is committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 in line with EU climate objectives.
The restoration of degraded peatlands will reduce greenhouse gas emissions by an estimated 1 million tonnes CO2 per year.
Emissions from drained peatlands must be reduced by 50% by 2030 as part of national climate commitments.
The strategy aims to reduce annual carbon dioxide emissions from peat extraction by at least 30% by 2030.
Rewetting of 40,000 hectares of degraded peatland will sequester an estimated 2.5 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent annually.
The target is to achieve net zero greenhouse gas emissions from the land use sector by 2050.
Carbon emissions from peat soils will be reduced through mandatory rewetting of all drained blanket bogs by 2035.
Peatland restoration will contribute to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Climate Action Plan targets.
In accordance with Article 6 of the Habitats Directive, an appropriate assessment must be carried out for all plans.
The Water Framework Directive requires member states to achieve good ecological status in all water bodies by 2027.
Under Regulation (EU) 2018/841, member states shall ensure that emissions from the land use sector do not exceed removals.
As required by the Birds Directive, member states shall designate Special Protection Areas for listed bird species.
Pursuant to the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive, all projects likely to have significant effects must be assessed.
In line with the EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030, member states shall restore at least 30% of degraded ecosystems.
Under the UNCCD, Parties shall develop national action programmes to combat land degradation and desertification.
The Convention on Biological Diversity requires parties to develop national biodiversity strategies and action plans.
This measure is required under the EU Nature Restoration Law which obliges member states to restore degraded habitats.
Member states shall report on progress towards land degradation neutrality targets under the UNCCD framework.
Turf-cutters affected by the cessation of cutting on raised bog SACs will be provided with a relocation package.
The government will provide alternative turbary plots to turf-cutters who can no longer cut on designated sites.
Training and upskilling opportunities will be provided to peatland workers transitioning to restoration activities.
Affected communities will receive practical assistance including access to alternative fuel supplies during the transition period.
A bog rehabilitation scheme will be established to provide landowners with practical support for restoration activities.
The government will deliver training to farmers on sustainable peatland management practices under the new scheme.
Conservation officers will be deployed to assist landowners with the practical implementation of restoration plans.
Peat soils cover approximately 21% of the national land area, representing around 1.47 million hectares.
Ireland has approximately 1.2 million hectares of peatland, of which around 310,000 hectares are designated as SACs.
The original extent of raised bogs in Ireland was estimated at 311,000 hectares before drainage and cutting.
About 9% of the land bank is already committed to wind energy use and this could grow to one-third or higher.
Scotland's peatlands cover approximately 1.8 million hectares, representing around 23% of total land area.
England's peatlands cover around 570,000 hectares including upland blanket bogs and lowland fens.
The plan may be revised where appropriate to reflect new scientific evidence on peatland extent and condition.
Restoration of peatlands could contribute significantly to climate mitigation if implemented at sufficient scale.
It is noted that peatland drainage has historically been encouraged through agricultural subsidy schemes.
Experience has shown that voluntary approaches alone are insufficient to achieve the necessary scale of restoration.
Further research may be needed to determine the most effective restoration techniques for different peatland types.
